title: Is GenAI revolutionizing court filings?
pub: National Center for State Courts — Court Statistics Project brief
author: National Center for State Courts

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source accepts that GenAI can lower barriers for unrepresented litigants while also enabling high-volume institutional filing, and materially extends the cluster by identifying resulting court-management demands and proposing monitoring and AI-assisted administration. It remains cautious about causally attributing filing trends to GenAI and does not establish improved remedies or outcomes.
qs: | National Center for State Courts  **  With ready access to many generative AI (GenAI) tools, filing court cases has become easier than ever, both for high volume filers, such as debt collection agencies, and for unrepresented litigants who may not be able to afford an attorney.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s cautious, workflow-specific framing and extends it to court administration and access-to-justice effects. It treats increased filings as correlational rather than proof of AI use, while proposing monitoring, validity checks and selective administrative AI—concrete applications of socio-technical evaluation and verification rather than autonomous reliance.

st.an: The source aligns with the synthesis by treating GenAI-driven filing growth as a tentative hypothesis rather than a demonstrated causal effect, while warning that easier, high-volume filing may burden courts and worsen default-heavy debt litigation. Its recommendations emphasize monitoring, safeguards and court preparedness rather than claiming improved access-to-justice outcomes.

kp.k: GenAI could lower barriers to self-represented civil litigation
kp.d: The brief argues that GenAI makes preparing court filings easier for people unable to afford counsel. Its illustrative scenario concerns a homeowner seeking to recover a $25,000 payment for unperformed work on a $50,000 renovation; the authors characterize the generated petition as usable with minor alterations. This is an illustration rather than evidence of actual filing outcomes, and the appendix's generated instructions recommend legal consultation.
qs: What does the homeowner get back? A decent petition that she can make minor alterations to and file with the court (Appendix A).
We believe there is possibility that those same tools might make it easier or more likely for self-represented litigants to file their own cases.
Consult with a lawyer to ensure the petition meets all legal requirements and that you follow the proper procedures to file it in court.

kp.k: High-volume debt collection creates potential AI amplification risks
kp.d: The brief reports Porcaro's 2023 argument that GenAI enables mass filing of low-value debt cases, with default judgments potentially allowing recovery even where filings contain errors. As background, it cites Oregon research finding that 10 plaintiffs account for more than half of filings and only four percent of defendants answer, and Michigan evidence that third-party collectors filed 60% of debt collection cases in 2019. These describe existing filing concentration and participation, not measured AI adoption.
qs: He argues that GenAI enables debt collection firms to file small value cases en masse, and because most of these cases end in default judgments, where the defendant never appears to challenge the case, even with errors, the plaintiff can collect.

In Oregon, 10 plaintiffs account for "more than half of all case filings and consisted entirely of third-party debt collectors, debt buyers, and national banks" and only four percent of defendants answer their case (McClendon & Kallattil, 2024).
In Michigan, third-party debt collectors filed 60% of debt collection cases in 2019.

kp.k: Study targets contract filings as potentially AI-sensitive cases
kp.d: The authors hypothesize that contract filings are particularly likely to increase with GenAI access because individual plaintiffs are less likely to have representation than in real estate and tort cases, while corporate plaintiffs include high-volume debt purchasers. They combine annual Court Statistics Project data with additional monthly data sought from Los Angeles County, Arkansas, Kentucky, Nevada, and Pennsylvania for 2023, 2024, and the first quarter of 2025 where available.
qs: We hypothesize that ready access to GenAI tools is likely to increase filings in contract cases, specifically, because:
Individual plaintiffs in contract case types are less likely to be represented than those in real estate and tort cases;
Corporate plaintiffs are often high-volume filers, such as debt purchasers.
These data included civil case filings by type and by month for 2023, 2024, and the first quarter of 2025 when available. Data were not available from all jurisdictions for all months.

kp.k: Annual civil filing growth is concentrated in contracts
kp.d: Court Statistics Project data show that civil caseloads remained below pre-pandemic levels, but increased 10.75% in 2023, the largest year-over-year increase since 2020. The brief attributes much of this growth to contract cases, which increased 21% in 2022 and 15% in 2023 across the 28 states supplying contract data for all five years. These are filing trends, not demonstrated effects of GenAI.
qs: civil caseloads have not yet returned to pre-pandemic levels.
However, the increase in 2023 was the largest year-over-year increase (10.75%) since 2020 (Figure 1).

This increase is largely driven by contract cases, where there was a 21% increase in 2022 and a 15% increase in 2023 for the 28 states able to provide data for contract cases across all five years (Figure 2).

kp.k: Monthly data show sustained contract growth through 2024
kp.d: For March 2023–December 2024, the monthly moving average of contract filings rose while tort, real property, and other civil categories were relatively flat. Contract filings in every month from March through December 2024 exceeded the corresponding 2023 month. Small claims were assigned to their underlying case type when available and otherwise to 'other'; January and February comparisons were omitted because not all states supplied those 2023 data.
qs: We can see an increase in the moving average of contract cases while the other case types are relatively flat.
We included small claims cases when the underlying case type was available but are otherwise categorized as "other."
In the other categories, including tort, real property, and other civil, the filings show no such consistent pattern.
Not all states provided data for January and February 2023, so those filings are not shown.

kp.d: The brief reports that available early-2025 contract filings equaled or exceeded 2024 levels in Arkansas, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, and Los Angeles County. Wisconsin was an exception: January 2025 exceeded January 2024, but the following three months were lower than their 2024 counterparts. The authors describe continuation of the growth trend tentatively.
qs: The trend seems to be continuing in 2025.
Figure 5 shows that 2025 contract filings, represented by the blue bars, are equaling or outpacing 2024 filings in Arkansas, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, and Los Angeles County.
In Wisconsin, January 2025 filings were higher than 2024, but lower in the following three months.

kp.k: Data cannot establish whether filers actually used AI
kp.d: The recent-data analysis uses a convenience sample of jurisdictions able to supply current filings. It does not examine specific case types within broad categories or county-level variation outside Los Angeles County. Critically, the authors lack both actual AI-use data and representation data, qualifying their interpretation of rising contract filings as support for a hypothesis connecting GenAI access and high-volume filings.
qs: This brief is based on a convenience sample, drawing data from a few of the jurisdictions where it was possible to get current data on filings.
We did not attempt to look at filings by specific case type within the larger case categories of contract, tort, real property, and other.
Critically, we have no data on whether any of these filers, whether individual or corporate plaintiffs, actually used AI to create their petitions.
Additionally, we do not have data on whether litigants were represented or not.

kp.k: Authors anticipate adoption without claiming definitive attribution
kp.d: The authors believe major filers are adopting or will shortly adopt AI, and interpret contract-specific growth as supporting their hypothesis of an association with GenAI access. Separately, Los Angeles County Superior Court CEO/Clerk David Slayton describes GenAI accessibility as a possible factor in rising civil filings, explicitly declining definitive attribution and urging courts to prepare for operational and policy consequences.
qs: We know that GenAI tools are proliferating, and we have reason to believe that the same filers responsible for the greatest volume in court filings are, or will shortly be, adopting AI tools.

The fact that we are seeing increases particularly in contract cases but not in real estate, tort, or other civil case types provides support to the hypothesis that increasing access to GenAI tools is correlated with increases in high volume case types.
While we cannot definitively attribute this trend to generative AI, it is reasonable to consider its growing accessibility as a possible factor.

kp.k: Courts should prepare capacity and strengthen debt-filing safeguards
kp.d: The brief recommends monitoring civil filings to allocate resources, implementing debt collection reforms, and considering AI for automatic filing-sufficiency checks and caseload management. Its heightened concern about validating debt lawsuits is conditional on the conjecture that GenAI is generating some petitions; the proposed court uses of AI are recommendations, not evaluated interventions.
qs: Courts should be prepared for increases in civil contract case filings.

If our conjecture is correct and GenAI tools are being used to generate some of these petitions, courts have an even greater obligation to ensure that debt lawsuits are valid (Consumer Debt Default Judgments Act, 2023; Rosenthal & Clerici, 2025; Spulak, 2023).
Monitor civil case filings to ensure that the court is allocating the resources necessary to manage these cases.
Consider using AI to automatically check case filings for sufficiency.
Consider using AI to help manage caseloads.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The NCSC brief claims GenAI makes preparing and filing civil cases easier and hypothesizes that its availability contributes to increasing contract-case filings.
pts.d: The brief describes two pathways: established high-volume corporate plaintiffs adopting AI, and individuals who cannot afford counsel using it to prepare their own petitions. Its homeowner example characterizes a GPT-4o-mini draft as a usable starting point after minor alterations. The authors believe the largest-volume filers are already adopting AI or will do so shortly, but describe increased self-represented filing more tentatively. They interpret growth concentrated in contract cases as support for their hypothesis, not as demonstrated AI causation. They advise courts to prepare for more contract filings and propose considering AI for filing-sufficiency checks and caseload management; these are recommendations rather than tested findings of effectiveness.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of descriptive filing trends, one illustrative AI-generated petition, and background research on debt-filing concentration; actual AI use by filers was not measured.
pts.d: Court Statistics Project data show civil filings rose 10.75% in 2023, the largest year-over-year increase since 2020, while remaining below pre-pandemic levels. For 28 states with five years of contract-case data, contract filings increased 21% in 2022 and 15% in 2023. More recent monthly data from a convenience sample show contract filings rising while other broad civil categories were relatively flat; March–December 2024 contract filings exceeded the corresponding 2023 months. Early 2025 data generally continued that pattern, with Wisconsin an exception after January. The GPT-4o-mini homeowner example illustrates drafting capability, not a measured filing outcome or systematic assessment of legal sufficiency. Cited Oregon and Michigan research establishes that debt litigation is concentrated among a few repeat plaintiffs and that participation by defendants can be low; it does not establish AI adoption. The brief explicitly lacks data on AI use and representation status, so its proposed AI–filing relationship remains a hypothesis.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The brief presents easier drafting as a current capability, high-volume-filer adoption as current or imminent, and further filing growth as a near-term possibility without a quantified forecast.
pts.d: The 2025 brief examines annual trends through 2023, monthly comparisons during 2023–2024, and available early-2025 data. Although the methodology refers to first-quarter 2025 availability, the findings describe Wisconsin's January and following three months. Coverage varies by jurisdiction and month; January and February are omitted from the 2023–2024 comparison because of missing data. The hypothesis particularly concerns contract cases because individual plaintiffs are less likely to have representation than in real-estate and tort cases, and corporate plaintiffs often file at high volume. The authors did not examine detailed subtypes within broad case categories or county-level variation outside Los Angeles County. Their AI-specific warning about validating debt lawsuits is explicitly conditional on AI actually being used. The sample petition's instructions also call for review, modification and consultation with a lawyer rather than unconditional reliance on the draft.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are self-represented civil plaintiffs, repeat corporate filers, debt defendants and courts.
pts.d: For individuals unable to afford counsel, the brief suggests AI drafting could make pursuing otherwise abandoned civil claims more feasible; its example involves a homeowner seeking recovery of a $25,000 contractor payment. For debt purchasers and other high-volume plaintiffs, AI could facilitate additional filing activity. Debt defendants face the corresponding importance of ensuring lawsuits are valid. The brief cites Porcaro's warning about erroneous mass filings resulting in default judgments as background argument, not as a finding of this study. Courts may face greater workloads, resource-allocation needs and pressure to implement debt-collection safeguards. Potential court-side AI applications include screening filings for sufficiency and managing caseloads, but the brief supplies no performance evidence for those applications. It does not forecast lawyer employment losses or changes in law-firm staffing.
